variants.name: Blocking write(2) on a pipe/socket (kernel-bounded)
variants.idiom_name: blocking write(2) + kernel pipe/socket buffer (or pthread mutex+condvar ring buffer in-process)
variants.implementation_notes: C has no flow-control abstraction, so the bounded hand-off is the kernel's own per-fd buffer: a blocking write(2) to a full pipe or socket simply blocks the writer until the reader drains, and that is the whole mechanism - correct for a producer that owns its thread. A pipe holds a fixed, non-negotiable capacity (16 pages by default on Linux, adjustable via fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ)), and a TCP socket is paced by the peer's receive window, so the bound exists but is not yours to size; never rely on a particular pipe capacity. For in-process stages there is no stdlib queue at all: the classic mutex + condition variable + bounded ring buffer (pthread_cond_wait/pthread_cond_signal) is hand-written, and it stays justified because the pattern really is a bound plus a blocking wait plus a full policy.
pitfalls: A blocking write in an event-loop thread stalls every other fd it is responsible for; either give the producer its own thread or move to the non-blocking form.
A write(2) to a pipe whose reader died raises SIGPIPE, which kills the process by default; ignore SIGPIPE or use send(MSG_NOSIGNAL) on sockets.

Blocking writes have no timeout: if the consumer never drains, the producer hangs forever, so pair the bound with a cancellation path (poll with a timeout, or a shutdown flag checked in the wait loop).
forgetting the not_full wait predicate (or using if instead of while) loses the bound under spurious wakeups and multiple producers.

variants.name: Non-blocking fd + EAGAIN + poll(POLLOUT)
variants.implementation_notes: When the producer must not block (single-threaded reactor, many fds, one thread), switch the fd to O_NONBLOCK, treat EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK as 'the buffer is full', and wait for POLLOUT via poll(2) or epoll before retrying - this is the POSIX-level equivalent of the demand signal, and the readiness loop replaces the blocking write. POLLOUT only promises that *some* space is available, so a partial write must be handled: the application keeps the unsent tail in its own bounded outbound buffer and re-registers for POLLOUT, which is exactly the classic structure the reactor-style code buys back. With multiple producers, POLLOUT can be level-triggered noisy; register interest only while the outbound queue is empty of unsent data.
pitfalls: POLLOUT readiness does not mean the whole buffer fits - loop the write and buffer the remainder, or bytes are silently lost.
Treating EAGAIN as an I/O error instead of the full signal turns backpressure into a crash.
epoll() with edge-triggered mode plus a partial write needs an explicit retry until EAGAIN, otherwise the fd never fires again.
Keeping POLLOUT registered while the outbound queue is empty busy-spins the loop.
